eruvin-7a-9-9.note: Rabbi Akiva picked the fruit of a citron tree on the first of the month of Shevat and set aside two different tithes from it: one following Beit Shammai, who count that day as the new year for trees, and one following Beit Hillel, who count it as still the old year.
eruvin-7a-9-9.why: Rav Sheizvi has said one may not take on two strict rulings that contradict each other. Rav Mesharshiya raises this incident against him, and the Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva was unsure which date Beit Hillel held, so he was strict both ways.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Set aside two tithes from one citron to satisfy both schools.

terms.meaning: A portion of produce that must be set aside. Which kind is due depends on the year of a seven-year cycle, so the date the fruit counts for matters.
A Hebrew month in mid-winter; the new year for trees falls in it.
Two early schools of Sages who disagreed on many laws.
A lemon-like fruit (etrog).

eruvin-8a-5-5.note: Rabbi Yitzhak told of an alleyway that ended at the sea on one side and at a refuse heap on the other. The case came before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to rule whether one could carry in it on Shabbat, and he said nothing about it, neither permitting nor forbidding.
eruvin-8a-5-5.why: Rav Mesharshiya cites this case to prove that a yard owned by one person is treated differently from one owned by many. The Gemara explains Rabbi's silence by the worry that the heap might be cleared or the sea might pile up sand.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Heard the case of the alleyway and gave no ruling either way.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: Reported the incident, as Ravin bar Rav Adda relates.

terms.meaning: A side street shared by several houses. Carrying in it on Shabbat is allowed only if it is closed off properly.
A garbage pile; if tall enough it can act as a wall, but it may be cleared away.

eruvin-11a-12-13.note: A man from the valley of Beit Hortan stuck four poles into the four corners of his field and stretched a vine over them. The case came before the Sages, and they permitted it for the laws of diverse kinds, treating the field as enclosed. Reish Lakish said that just as they permitted it for diverse kinds, they permitted it for Shabbat. Rabbi Yohanan said they permitted it for diverse kinds but not for Shabbat.
eruvin-11a-12-13.why: The Gemara wants to show that Rabbi Yohanan agrees with Rav that a doorway-shaped frame does not close an opening wider than ten cubits; it argues that only such wide gaps explain his refusal for Shabbat.

people.name: a man from the valley of Beit Hortan
people.about: Fenced his field with four poles and a vine.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Held the Sages' permission applied to Shabbat too.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Held the permission applied only to diverse kinds, not to Shabbat.

terms.meaning: The Torah ban on planting certain crops together, such as grain next to a vineyard. A proper partition between them removes the problem.
Two upright poles with a crosspiece on top; in Jewish law it can count as a wall with an opening.

eruvin-11b-12-12.note: Rav Nahman built a doorway frame at the Exilarch's house following his own opinion, with the top reed not touching the side reeds. Rav Sheshet told his attendant Rav Gadda: go, pull them out and throw them away. He went, pulled them out and threw them away. The Exilarch's household found him and imprisoned him. Rav Sheshet went and stood at the door and called: Gadda, come out! And he came out and came to him.
eruvin-11b-12-12.why: Rav Nahman and Rav Sheshet have just disagreed over whether the side reeds of a doorway frame must touch the top reed for it to count; the story shows them acting out that dispute.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Built a doorway frame at the Exilarch's house by his own ruling.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Disagreed with Rav Nahman and had the frame torn down.

people.name: Rav Gadda
people.about: Rav Sheshet's attendant, who pulled out the reeds and was jailed for it.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, with his own court and household.
Two upright reeds with one across the top; in Jewish law it can count as a closed side, allowing carrying on Shabbat.

eruvin-11b-27-27.note: Rabbi Eliezer went to visit his disciple Rabbi Yosei ben Perida in the town of Ovelin and found him living in an alleyway that had only one side post. He told him: My son, set up another side post. The disciple answered: Am I required to close it up? Rabbi Eliezer replied: Let it be closed up; what does it matter?
eruvin-11b-27-27.why: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Eliezer wants two side posts plus a cross beam, or two side posts alone. It reads the disciple's 'close it up' as showing a cross beam was also required, then rejects the proof: he may have meant closing it with side posts.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A teacher who visits his disciple and tells him to add a second side post to his alleyway.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Perida
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's disciple, living in Ovelin in an alleyway with only one side post.

terms.meaning: An upright post at the entrance of an alleyway. It marks the alley off from the public street so that people may carry objects within it on Shabbat.
A collection of early rabbinic teachings from the same period as the Mishna, often adding cases and details the Mishna leaves out.

eruvin-13a-7-9.note: Rabbi Meir, a scribe who wrote Torah scrolls, studied with two great teachers, Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva. In one account he put iron sulfate in his ink, and Rabbi Yishmael said nothing while Rabbi Akiva forbade it. In a second account it is the reverse: Rabbi Yishmael asked his trade, warned him that adding or leaving out one letter could destroy the whole world, and when Meir said he used iron sulfate so his ink would not be erased, Yishmael objected that the Torah requires writing that can be blotted out.
eruvin-13a-7-9.why: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi has just said that the unnamed disciple who studied under both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is Rabbi Meir; this teaching is brought to show he served both. The Gemara then notes the two accounts disagree on which teacher came first and which one forbade the ink.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A scribe of Torah scrolls who studied under both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: One of Rabbi Meir's teachers; in one account he warns him to take great care as a scribe.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Meir's other teacher; the two accounts disagree on whether he forbade the iron sulfate.

terms.meaning: A chemical added to ink that makes it permanent and hard to erase.
A teaching from the early rabbinic period that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Talmud discusses.
A wife suspected by her husband of adultery. In the Torah's ritual, a priest writes curses on a scroll and dissolves the writing into water she drinks, which is why that ink must be erasable.

eruvin-13b-9-10.note: For three years the two great schools, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, disagreed, each saying the law followed its own view. Then a Divine Voice came out and declared that both are the words of the living God, but the law follows Beit Hillel. The Gemara asks why Beit Hillel won, and answers that they were agreeable and forbearing, taught their opponents' views alongside their own, and even mentioned Beit Shammai's opinion first.
eruvin-13b-9-10.why: The discussion has just praised a student so clever he could argue a creeping animal pure. This story says Beit Hillel won the law through humility, not sharpness, and the Gemara goes on to show them naming Beit Shammai's elders first in a mishna.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Reports this account in the name of Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage in whose name the account is told.

terms.meaning: The two leading schools of early rabbinic law, named for their founders Shammai and Hillel, who disagreed on hundreds of questions.
A voice from heaven that, in rabbinic stories, announces God's will or settles a matter.
Jewish law; the ruling people actually follow in practice.

eruvin-15a-16-16.note: Rav was sitting in an alleyway with his student Rav Huna, and sent his attendant to bring a pitcher of water. While the attendant was gone, the side post at the alley's entrance fell down. Rav signaled with his hand, and the attendant stopped where he stood. Rav Huna asked why they could not rely on the palm tree at the entrance as a side post. Rav said Rav Huna was like someone who does not know the Sages' teachings: they had not relied on the palm tree since yesterday.
eruvin-15a-16-16.why: The Gemara is debating whether something not put up to be a side post can count as one. It infers from Rav's answer that had they relied on the palm tree before Shabbat, it would have been valid.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage sitting in the alleyway who stops his attendant once the side post falls.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Sits before Rav and asks why the palm tree cannot serve as the side post.

terms.meaning: An upright post at the entrance of an alleyway. It marks the alley off from the public street so that people may carry objects within it on Shabbat; without it, carrying there is forbidden.
A narrow lane shared by several houses that opens onto a public street. Special rules decide when carrying is allowed in it on Shabbat.

eruvin-16b-26-28.note: Rav Nahman taught in public, in Shmuel's name, that one traveler or two may enclose two beit se'a with ropes, and three, who count as a caravan, may enclose six. He was asked whether he had abandoned the majority of the Rabbis to follow the lone view of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda. Rav Nahman then set up a speaker beside him and announced: What I told you was my error. Three people get as much space as they need. The Gemara then explains that the first half still follows Rabbi Yosei because his father, Rabbi Yehuda, held the same view.
eruvin-16b-26-28.why: The Gemara has been comparing Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, with the Rabbis on how much space ropes may enclose for travelers. Rav Nahman's public correction shows which view the law follows for a caravan.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Teaches a ruling in Shmuel's name, then publicly retracts part of it as his own error.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage in whose name Rav Nahman first taught, called here 'Rabbeinu', our teacher.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: An early Sage whose minority view Rav Nahman was accused of following.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Father of Rabbi Yosei; the Gemara says he held the same view as his son.

terms.meaning: An area of land, the space in which a se'a of seed is sown; roughly 50 by 50 cubits. Two beit se'a is the standard size of an enclosure one may carry in on Shabbat.
A group of three or more travelers, who are given more space to enclose for carrying on Shabbat than one or two people.
A man who stood by a teacher and repeated his words aloud to the audience. Setting one up made Rav Nahman's correction an official public lecture.

eruvin-21a-10-11.note: Rav Hisda said to Marei, son of Rav Huna and grandson of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba: People say you walk on Shabbat from Barnish to Daniel's synagogue, three parasangs away. What do you rely on, the huts at the edge of town? Your own grandfather said in Rav's name that the law of huts does not apply in Babylonia. Marei went out and showed him a line of ruined towns, each within seventy cubits and a bit of the next, which he relied on instead.
eruvin-21a-10-11.why: The Gemara has just cited Rav, through Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, that huts do not extend the Shabbat boundary in Babylonia. Rav Hisda tests the grandson against his grandfather's ruling, and Marei shows he relied on something else.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Questions Marei about his long Shabbat walk.

people.name: Marei
people.about: Son of Rav Huna and grandson of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba; walks from Barnish to Daniel's synagogue on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: Marei's grandfather, who reported in Rav's name that the law of huts does not apply in Babylonia.

terms.meaning: A Persian unit of distance, about four miles. Three parasangs is far beyond the normal 2,000-cubit walking limit on Shabbat.
Simple dwellings outside a town. Where they count as homes, the town's Shabbat boundary is measured from them, letting people walk farther.
The distance, about seventy and two-thirds cubits, within which separate settlements are treated as one town when measuring the Shabbat walking limit.

eruvin-21b-11-14.note: Rabbi Akiva was held in prison, and Rabbi Yehoshua HaGarsi looked after him, bringing a measured amount of water each day. One day the guard said the water was too much, perhaps to dig through the prison wall, and poured out half. When Rabbi Akiva saw how little there was, he said: Do you not know I am old and my life depends on yours? Hearing what happened, he still asked for water to wash his hands. Rabbi Yehoshua protested that there was not enough even to drink. Rabbi Akiva said it was better to die his own death than go against his colleagues' ruling, and he tasted nothing until he had washed. The Sages said: if he is so careful in old age and in prison, how much more so in youth and in freedom.
eruvin-21b-11-14.why: The Gemara has been stressing how weighty the words of the Sages are, saying that whoever mocks them is punished. Handwashing before eating is one of their rules, and right after the story the Gemara credits King Solomon with instituting it.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Imprisoned and old; insists on washing his hands before eating even when water is scarce.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua HaGarsi
people.about: Attends to Rabbi Akiva in prison and brings him his daily water.

terms.meaning: A ritual rinsing of the hands before eating bread, enacted by the Sages. Rabbi Akiva here treats breaking it as deserving death.
A teaching from the early rabbinic period that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Talmud discusses.

eruvin-22a-1-1.note: Rav Adda bar Mattana was about to leave for the study hall when his wife asked him: What shall I do for your children? He answered: Are all the rushes in the marsh already gone? Let them eat those.
eruvin-22a-1-1.why: The Gemara is reading 'black as a raven' in the Song of Songs as describing who keeps the Torah. Rava says it is one who is cruel to his family like a raven for the Torah's sake, and this exchange is his example.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: A scholar who leaves for the study hall and tells his wife to feed the children rushes.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who gives this as an example of making oneself cruel to one's household for Torah.

terms.meaning: Marsh plants, a poor famine food. Rav Adda is saying the children can eat those if there is nothing else.

eruvin-25a-22-22.note: A woman built a partition on top of an existing partition on land that had belonged to a convert who died. Then a man came and plowed the ground a little. He brought the matter to Rav Nahman, who ruled the land belonged to him. The woman came and cried out before Rav Nahman, and he told her: What can I do for you? You did not take possession the way people take possession.
eruvin-25a-22-22.why: The Gemara has been discussing partitions added on top of existing ones, and whether they count. This case from property law shows Rav Nahman did not count such added building as a real act of taking ownership.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who awards the land to the man who plowed it.

terms.meaning: A convert who died with no Jewish heirs left property that belonged to no one, so the first person to take possession of it could acquire it.
Doing something to ownerless land, such as working it, that legally makes it yours.

eruvin-25b-7-8.note: An orchard bordered on the wall of a mansion, and that wall also served as one of the orchard's walls. The mansion's outer wall collapsed. Rav Beivai thought the mansion's inner walls could be used as the orchard's wall instead. Rav Pappi mocked him: Because you come from truncated people, you say truncated things. Those walls were built for the inside of the mansion, not for the outside.
eruvin-25b-7-8.why: The Gemara has been asking whether a fallen wall leaves an enclosure in which carrying is still allowed. This case asks whether walls built for another purpose, the mansion's interior, can close the gap; Rav Pappi says they cannot.

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: Proposes using the mansion's inner walls to enclose the orchard.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: Rejects Rav Beivai's idea with a cutting pun about his family.

terms.meaning: A pun. The translation explains that Rav Beivai's family descended from the priest Eli, whose descendants were said to die young, so Rav Pappi calls his idea 'cut short' too.

eruvin-25b-9-10.note: The Exilarch had a banqueting pavilion in his orchard and asked Rav Huna bar Hinnana to arrange for them to eat there the next day, Shabbat. Rav Huna bar Hinnana put up fences of reeds set less than three handbreadths apart. Rava went and pulled them out, and his students Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, gathered up the reeds after him. The next day Ravina, then Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, each raised objections to Rava, showing the fences had been needed. The Exilarch applied a verse to them: They are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge.
eruvin-25b-9-10.why: The Gemara has been asking when a large enclosure counts as enclosed for living, which permits carrying. Rava treated the orchard as residential because of the pavilion; the objections from new and old towns and from privacy screens argue it was not.

people.name: Exilarch
people.about: Owner of the orchard and pavilion, who wanted to eat there on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hinnana
people.about: Builds the reed fences at the Exilarch's request.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Removes the reed fences, judging them unnecessary.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Rava's student; collects the reeds, then the next day raises an objection to Rava.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Objects to Rava the next day from the rule about new and old towns.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, a powerful leader with his own court.
A measure of about the width of a palm. Reeds set less than three handbreadths apart count in Jewish law as a solid wall.
A legal arrangement that joins several homes or courtyards into one shared space, so that people may carry between them on Shabbat.
The distance one may walk outside a town on Shabbat, measured from its edge; the new-town and old-town rule decides where that edge is.

eruvin-28b-2-3.note: When Rabbi Zeira was too tired to study, he would sit at the entrance of Rav Yehuda bar Ami's academy, so he could stand up for the Sages as they came and went and earn reward for honoring them. Once a schoolchild came out, and Rabbi Zeira asked what his teacher had taught him. The child said the blessing over dodder is 'Who creates the fruit of the ground', and over green grain 'By Whose word all things came to be'. Rabbi Zeira said the opposite made more sense, since green grain draws its food from the ground and dodder from the air.
eruvin-28b-2-3.why: The Gemara has just discussed green grain as food for an eiruv. After the story it rules that the law follows the child: dodder is fully ripened produce and green grain is not, and dodder does draw from the ground, since it dies when its host shrub is cut.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who rests at an academy door to honor scholars and questions a schoolchild.

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Ami
people.about: Head of the academy at whose entrance Rabbi Zeira sits.

terms.meaning: A climbing plant that wraps around a shrub and lives off it.
A short praise of God said before eating. The wording depends on the food: produce of the ground gets one blessing, other foods a general one.

eruvin-29b-2-2.note: Rabbi Hanina once ate half an onion along with half of its toxins. He fell deathly ill. His colleagues prayed for mercy for him, and he lived, because the times needed him.
eruvin-29b-2-2.why: The Gemara is asking whether onions can be used for an eiruv, and has explained that onion leaves can be deadly. This teaching, warning against eating onion, adds a case of a Sage nearly killed by one.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage who nearly died after eating an onion and recovered after his colleagues prayed for him.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early rabbinic period that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Talmud discusses.
His generation needed his teaching, so he was spared; otherwise, the text implies, he would not have recovered.

eruvin-34b-7-7.note: An army came to Neharde'a and took over the study hall, leaving the students no room. Rav Nahman told them: Go out to the marshes and make seats by pressing down reeds, and tomorrow, on Shabbat, we will go and sit on them.
eruvin-34b-7-7.why: The mishna says an eiruv placed on a reed counts only if the reed was cut and stuck back in the ground. Rav Nahman's instruction is challenged from that mishna, and he answers that the mishna is about hard reeds, while soft ones may be bent and used.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage in Neharde'a who tells his students to make reed seats in the marsh for Shabbat study.

terms.meaning: Bending growing reeds down and binding them into seats before Shabbat, since using growing plants on Shabbat itself is restricted.

eruvin-39b-6-11.note: A deer was brought to the Exilarch's house, caught on the first day of a Diaspora Festival and slaughtered on the second. Rav Nahman and Rav Hisda ate it; Rav Sheshet refused. Rav Nahman joked: What can I do for Rav Sheshet, who will not eat deer? Rav Sheshet cited Isi's teaching that Rabbi Yosei forbids this on the two Diaspora Festival days. Later Rabba bar Shmuel told Rav Sheshet he had learned that Rabbi Yosei agrees about those two days, and Rav Sheshet said: If you meet them, tell them nothing. Rav Ashi reported, in Ameimar's name, that the deer was not caught on the Festival but brought from outside the Shabbat limit; in that version, the Gemara says, the meeting never happened.
eruvin-39b-6-11.why: A teaching just cited has Rabbi Yosei forbid treating the two Diaspora Festival days as separate, even with a condition. The deer case tests whether a Sage may rely on one of those days being an ordinary weekday.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Eats the deer and teases Rav Sheshet for refusing.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Eats the deer together with Rav Nahman.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Refuses to eat the deer, citing a teaching attributed to Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rabba bar Shmuel
people.about: Tells Rav Sheshet a teaching that would undercut his refusal.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: Tells Rav Ashi a different version: the deer was brought from outside the Shabbat limit.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who often hosted the Sages at his table.

terms.term: two Festival days of the Diaspora
terms.meaning: Outside the Land of Israel, each Festival was kept for two days because of doubt about the calendar, so one of the two was really an ordinary day.
The distance, 2,000 cubits beyond a town, that one may walk or carry things on Shabbat or a Festival. Food brought from beyond it on the holy day may be forbidden.

eruvin-40a-3-5.note: On a Festival, a delivery of turnips arrived in the town of Mehoza. Rava went out, saw that they were withered, and allowed people to buy them, saying they must have been pulled up the day before. Even if they came from outside the Shabbat limit, what is brought for one Jew is permitted to another, and these were brought for gentiles. But once Rava saw the merchants bringing more and more turnips, he forbade them.
eruvin-40a-3-5.why: The Gemara has just explained that the Sages disagreed over the deer at the Exilarch's house about whether food brought from outside the limit for one person is allowed to others. Rava's ruling applies that principle, and shows its limit once goods are brought for Jews.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage in Mehoza who first permits buying the turnips and later forbids it.

terms.meaning: The distance, 2,000 cubits beyond a town, that one may walk or carry things on Shabbat or a Festival. Goods brought from beyond it for a Jew on the holy day are forbidden to him.
A biblical holy day, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which most work is forbidden as on Shabbat.

eruvin-40a-6-7.note: Some canopy makers cut myrtle branches on the second day of a Festival, and that evening Ravina allowed people to smell them right away. Rava bar Tahalifa told Ravina to forbid it, since these men were not learned in Torah. Rav Shemaya objected: even for the learned, don't we require waiting as long as it would take to cut them? They went and asked Rava, who said: We require that wait.
eruvin-40a-6-7.why: The Gemara is collecting cases of goods prepared or brought on a Festival and when they may be used. This one asks whether people must wait after the Festival for the time it took to do the forbidden work.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Permits smelling the myrtles immediately after the Festival.

people.name: Rava bar Tahalifa
people.about: Urges Ravina to forbid it because the canopy makers are not learned.

people.name: Rav Shemaya
people.about: Argues that a waiting period applies to everyone.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules that one must wait as long as it took to cut the myrtles.

terms.meaning: Outside the Land of Israel, each Festival was kept for two days because of doubt about the calendar.
After a holy day ends, something made forbiddenly on it may be used only after waiting as long as it would take to do that work.

eruvin-40b-15-15.note: The Sages sent Rav Yeimar the Elder to Rav Hisda on the eve of Rosh HaShana, telling him to watch what he did and report back. When Rav Hisda saw him, he quoted a folk saying: One who picks up a damp log wants to do something on the spot, meaning: you have come for a reason. They brought him a cup of wine, and he recited kiddush and the blessing for time.
eruvin-40b-15-15.why: The Gemara has been asking whether the blessing for time is said on Rosh HaShana and Yom Kippur, and how, since one cannot drink wine on Yom Kippur. Rav Hisda's practice settles it: the blessing is said on both days, even without wine.

people.name: Rav Yeimar the Elder
people.about: Sent by the Sages to see how Rav Hisda conducts himself on the eve of Rosh HaShana.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Recites kiddush and the blessing for time over wine as Rav Yeimar watches.

terms.meaning: A blessing said over a cup of wine at the start of Shabbat or a Festival, declaring the day holy.
The blessing thanking God 'Who has given us life' and brought us to this season, said at the start of a Festival.
The Jewish New Year, a two-day holy day in the autumn.

eruvin-41a-5-5.note: After Rabban Gamliel died, Rabbi Yehoshua came into the study hall to overturn his ruling on fasts. Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri stood up and said: The body follows the head. All of Rabban Gamliel's life we fixed the law according to him, and now you want to cancel his words? Yehoshua, we will not listen to you; the law has been fixed according to Rabban Gamliel. And no one disputed this at all.
eruvin-41a-5-5.why: Ulla rules with Rabbi Yosei that a Ninth of Av fast falling on Friday is completed; Rabban Gamliel's view, as Rabbi Meir reports it, is that it is not. The Gemara cites this to show Rabban Gamliel's ruling became law, then answers that in Rabbi Yosei's time people followed Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Leader of the Sages, whose rulings were followed throughout his life; the story begins after his death.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Tries to overturn Rabban Gamliel's ruling after his death.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
people.about: Stands up to defend Rabban Gamliel's ruling against Rabbi Yehoshua.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early rabbinic period that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Talmud discusses.
A saying meaning the community should follow its established leaders and the rulings already fixed by them.

eruvin-43b-10-10.note: Rabban Gamliel and others were traveling by boat, and it did not reach port until after nightfall on Friday, when Shabbat had begun. They asked Rabban Gamliel whether they could get off. He said they could, because he had been watching and knew they had come within the city's limit before nightfall, so they could walk anywhere in the city.
eruvin-43b-10-10.why: Right afterward the Gemara explains how Rabban Gamliel could tell: he had a tube he looked through to judge 2,000 cubits on land and the same distance at sea.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Rules that the passengers may leave the boat, having watched when it came within the city's limit.

terms.meaning: On Shabbat one may walk 2,000 cubits beyond the place where one was when Shabbat began. Arriving inside that range before nightfall let the passengers go through the whole city.

eruvin-44b-4-4.note: Members of a wedding party wanted to bring water in on Shabbat from a public area into a private one, and they did it by lining up the many people present as a wall, with the people knowing they were being used that way. Shmuel ordered the wedding party to be flogged. He asked: if the Sages allowed a human wall when the people do not know what they are being used for, does that mean they would allow it when the people know?
eruvin-44b-4-4.why: The Gemara has just drawn a line between people who serve as a wall knowingly, which is forbidden, and unknowingly, which is allowed. Shmuel's punishment of the wedding party shows the forbidden side of that line in practice.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who ordered the wedding party flogged for using people knowingly as a wall.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, on which carrying objects from a public area into a private one is forbidden.
A wall or barrier that changes the legal status of an area for carrying on Shabbat. Here the 'wall' is made of standing people.
Whipped as a punishment imposed by the Sages for breaking their rules.

eruvin-44b-5-5.note: Some flasks were lying in the marketplace of Mehoza on Shabbat, where they could not be moved. When Rava came back from giving his public lecture, a crowd walked with him, and his attendants used the crowd as a human wall to carry the flasks into his house. On another Shabbat they wanted to do the same thing, but Rava forbade it: this time the people would know what they were being used for, and that is forbidden.
eruvin-44b-5-5.why: The discussion has drawn a line between people who unknowingly serve as a wall, which is allowed, and those who knowingly do, which is forbidden. Rava's two Shabbats show the same act landing on both sides of that line.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage returning from his lecture; his attendants used the crowd around him to bring the flasks into his house.

terms.meaning: The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, on which carrying objects from a public area into a private one is forbidden.
A town in Babylonia, where Rava lived.
A row of people treated as a wall, which can make carrying on Shabbat permitted in certain cases.

eruvin-45a-8-9.note: Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, explains that those who go out to save lives on Shabbat may come home carrying their weapons, and cites an old teaching about how this came about. At first, defenders returning from a rescue would leave their weapons in the first house by the town wall. Once, enemies noticed they were unarmed and chased them; the defenders rushed into the house for their weapons, the enemies followed them in, and in the crush they killed more of each other than the enemies killed. After that the Sages ruled that defenders return to their places with their weapons.
eruvin-45a-8-9.why: The Gemara asked whether rescuers may walk home more than the usual two thousand cubits on Shabbat. Rav's answer reads the permission as being about carrying weapons home, and this disaster explains why that permission was given.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Sage who reports Rav's explanation and the old teaching behind it.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose explanation Rav Yehuda quotes.

terms.meaning: A collection of early rabbinic teachings, from the same period as the Mishna, quoted here as the source of the story.
The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, on which carrying and walking far are restricted, though saving lives overrides these rules.

eruvin-45a-20-21.note: Rabbi Yehuda tells of Rabbi Tarfon, who was traveling on the eve of Shabbat when night fell, so he spent the night outside a town. In the morning, cowherds found him and said: Master, the town is right in front of you, go in. He went in, sat in the study hall, and taught all day.
eruvin-45a-20-21.why: The Mishna records a dispute: Rabbi Meir says a traveler who did not mean to settle near a town may not enter it on Shabbat; Rabbi Yehuda says he may, citing Rabbi Tarfon. The other Sages reply that Tarfon may have intended it, or the study hall was within his limit.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A Sage who slept outside a town on Shabbat and entered it in the morning when cowherds urged him to.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who tells the story about Rabbi Tarfon.

terms.meaning: On Shabbat a person may walk only about two thousand cubits (roughly a kilometer) from where he was when Shabbat began; a town may lie inside or outside that range.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the main collection of their rulings.
The house where the Sages and their students gathered to learn and teach Torah.

eruvin-47b-0-0.note: Rabbi Yosei reports that Yosef the priest left the Land of Israel and went to his teacher in Tzeidan, outside the land, to learn Torah. The translation adds that the leading Sage of the time, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, was living in the Land of Israel.
eruvin-47b-0-0.why: The question is whether a priest may leave the Land of Israel, and become ritually impure, to study Torah when there is a teacher at home. Rabbi Yosei says yes, since not everyone can learn from every teacher, and cites Yosef the priest. Rabbi Yohanan rules like Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Yosef the priest
people.about: A priest who went to his teacher in Tzeidan, outside the Land of Israel, to study Torah.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who tells about Yosef the priest to support his view.

terms.meaning: A descendant of Aaron (a kohen). Priests must avoid ritual impurity, and the Sages treated lands outside Israel as impure.
Sidon, a city on the coast north of the Land of Israel.

eruvin-47b-12-15.note: Rams were brought on Shabbat to the town of Mavrakhta, and Rava allowed the people of Mehoza to buy them and take them home. Ravina challenged him: you must be relying on Shmuel, who said a gentile's property is not tied to a Shabbat location, but the law follows Rabbi Yohanan, who said it is. Rava changed his ruling: the rams could be sold only to the people of Mavrakhta itself, since for them the whole town counts as the animals' own small area.
eruvin-47b-12-15.why: The Gemara has just set out the dispute over whether objects owned by a gentile are fixed to a Shabbat location, with Rabbi Yohanan saying they are. The case of the rams shows the dispute decided in practice in Rabbi Yohanan's favor.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who first let the people of Mehoza buy the rams, then took back that ruling.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Sage who challenged Rava's ruling.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage cited for the view that a gentile's property does not acquire a Shabbat location.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage cited for the view that it does; the law follows him.

terms.meaning: When Shabbat begins, people and objects become tied to where they are and may be moved only within a set range of that spot.
The small area, about two meters, within which something outside its permitted range may still be moved on Shabbat.
The distance, two thousand cubits, beyond a town that a person may walk on Shabbat.

eruvin-48a-15-18.note: Rav Mesharshiya gave his son a question to ask Rav Pappa: are a person's four cubits on Shabbat measured by his own forearm, or by the standard measure? He even prepared the follow-up challenges for either answer, including what to do about the giant Og, king of Bashan. When the son asked, Rav Pappa answered that if we were that precise we could never study anything. He then ruled that each person's own forearm is the measure, and explained why the rule was left off the list of measures that vary from person to person: some people have short limbs for their bodies.
eruvin-48a-15-18.why: The Gemara has been asking where the four cubits a person may always move within on Shabbat come from and how big they are. Rav Mesharshiya's question pushes on exactly how they are measured.

people.name: Rav Mesharshiya
people.about: Sage who sent his son with a question for Rav Pappa.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Sage who answered the question.

people.name: Og, king of the Bashan
people.about: A giant king from the Bible, raised as a test case for the measurement.

terms.meaning: A unit of length based on the forearm, from elbow to fingertip, roughly half a meter.
A fixed, standard cubit used in Temple matters, the same for everyone.
The small area around a person in which he may always move on Shabbat, even when he may not walk anywhere else.

eruvin-51b-7-7.note: Rabbi Yehuda tells of the households of Memel and Guryon in the village of Aroma, who handed out dried figs and raisins to the poor in years of famine. The poor of the villages of Sihin and Hananya would walk to the edge of their Shabbat limit by nightfall on Friday, and early the next morning they would set off and come to collect the food.
eruvin-51b-7-7.why: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree over who may fix his Shabbat base far from home just by standing there. Rabbi Yehuda says even someone with a home and food may, and cites the paupers walking to Aroma as precedent.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who tells the story to support his view.

people.name: Memel and Guryon households
people.about: Families in Aroma who gave figs and raisins to the poor during famine.

terms.meaning: A legal device that lets a person on Shabbat walk further than usual by fixing his base at another spot, either by placing food there or by standing there.
The distance, two thousand cubits, a person may walk beyond his town on Shabbat.

eruvin-51b-13-13.note: Rabba bar Rav Hanan used to walk on Shabbat from his home in Artibbena to Pumbedita, and to do it he would declare from home on Friday: my Shabbat base is in Tzinta, a place between the two. Abaye challenged him: you are relying on Rabbi Yehuda as Rav Hisda explained him, but Rav Nahman explained the dispute differently, and a teaching supports Rav Nahman. Rabba bar Rav Hanan said: I take back my view.
eruvin-51b-13-13.why: Rav has just ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, who lets even a person at home fix his base elsewhere. Rabba bar Rav Hanan acted on a wide reading of that, and Abaye uses Rav Nahman's reading, backed by a baraita, to show it does not reach so far.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Hanan
people.about: Sage who walked on Shabbat from Artibbena to Pumbedita by declaring his base in Tzinta.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who challenged his practice.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Sage whose explanation of the dispute Rabba bar Rav Hanan relied on.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage who explained the dispute differently, in a way that rules out the practice.

terms.meaning: A spoken declaration that fixes a person's Shabbat base at a spot other than his home, so he can walk two thousand cubits from there.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

eruvin-52a-16-16.note: Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata brought a basket of fruit on the eve of Shabbat to Rav Natan bar Oshaya, who lived in another town. As he was leaving, Rav Natan let him go down one step and then said: stay here tonight. The next morning Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata rose early and walked home. The Gemara asks which Sages' views Rav Natan's action followed, and gives two possible answers.
eruvin-52a-16-16.why: The Gemara has been working out Ulla's ruling that a man who set out on his journey and was then persuaded to turn back still counts as having set out. Rav Natan's move, letting his guest start out before asking him to stay, looks like that ruling in action.

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata
people.about: Sage who brought fruit to Rav Natan bar Oshaya and stayed the night.

people.name: Rav Natan bar Oshaya
people.about: The host who let his guest step out before asking him to stay.

terms.meaning: Having actually started a journey before Shabbat, which can let a traveler fix his Shabbat base along the road and so reach home the next day.

eruvin-53b-7-7.note: A woman came before a judge meaning to say: Master, sir, I had a board and it was stolen from me. Because she mispronounced her words, what she actually said was: Master, servant, I had a beam and they stole you from me, and it was so big that when they hung you on it your feet did not reach the ground.
eruvin-53b-7-7.why: The Gemara is contrasting the precise speech of the people of Judea with the careless speech of Galileans, and this is one of several examples of Galileans whose mispronunciation turned their words into nonsense or insult.

terms.meaning: People of the Galilee, in northern Israel, whose speech the Gemara describes here as imprecise, especially in pronouncing certain letters.

eruvin-53b-17-19.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya said that no one ever got the better of him in words except a woman, a young boy and a young girl. The woman was his hostess at an inn. She served him beans, and the first two days he ate them all without leaving any on his plate. On the third day she over-salted them, and he stopped eating. When she asked why, he politely said he had already eaten during the day; she said he should have held back from bread then, and asked whether he was now leaving food because he had not left any the first days, as the Sages say a guest should leave some on the plate.
eruvin-53b-17-19.why: The Gemara has been collecting examples of clever and witty speech, and this is the first of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya's three tales of being outwitted.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage who tells of the few times he was beaten in a verbal exchange.

people.name: the hostess
people.about: The woman who ran the inn where he stayed and who over-salted his beans.

terms.meaning: Good manners of the time: a guest left a little food on his plate rather than clearing it.

eruvin-53b-20-20.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya tells how a young girl got the better of him. He was walking along a path that crossed a field, and a girl said to him: Rabbi, isn't this a field? He answered that it was a well-trodden path. She said: robbers like you have trodden it.
eruvin-53b-20-20.why: This is the second of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya's three tales of being beaten in words, after the hostess and before the young boy, in a run of stories about clever speech.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage who tells of the times he was outwitted.

people.name: a young girl
people.about: The girl who rebuked him for walking through a field.

terms.meaning: A path already beaten through a field, where walking does no further harm to crops and so is allowed.

eruvin-53b-21-22.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya tells how a young boy got the better of him. He met the boy at a crossroads and asked the way to the city. The boy said one road was short and long, the other long and short. He took the short-and-long road, but near the city found it ringed by gardens and orchards he could not get through. He went back and said: my son, didn't you tell me this way was short? The boy answered: and didn't I tell you it was long? He kissed the boy on the head and said: happy are you, Israel, for you are all very wise, from old to young.
eruvin-53b-21-22.why: This is the third of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya's three tales of being beaten in words, in a run of stories about clever speech.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage who tells of the times he was outwitted.

people.name: a young boy
people.about: The boy at the crossroads who gave him a riddling answer about the way to the city.

eruvin-53b-23-23.note: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili was walking along the road when he met Berurya, and asked her: by which road shall we go to Lod? She answered: foolish Galilean, didn't the Sages say, do not talk much with a woman? You should have said: which way to Lod?
eruvin-53b-23-23.why: The Gemara has been telling stories of clever speech and of the wisdom of women; Berurya's retort follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya's tales and uses the familiar jibe at Galileans' wordiness.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
people.about: A Sage from the Galilee who asked Berurya the way to Lod.

people.name: Berurya
people.about: A learned woman who mocked his wordy question.

terms.meaning: Someone from the Galilee in northern Israel; the discussion has been teasing Galileans for careless speech.
A town in the Land of Israel, also known as Lydda.

eruvin-53b-24-24.note: Berurya came across a student who was whispering his studies instead of saying them aloud. She kicked him and quoted the verse 'ordered in all things and secure': if the Torah is set in all of your 248 limbs, it stays with you, and if not, it does not. The Gemara adds a teaching that Rabbi Eliezer had a student who studied quietly and after three years forgot what he had learned.
eruvin-53b-24-24.why: This follows another story of Berurya's wit, and leads into Shmuel's advice to Rav Yehuda to open his mouth when he studies so that his learning lasts.

people.name: Berurya
people.about: A learned woman who kicked a student for studying in a whisper.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage whose quiet-studying student forgot his learning after three years.

terms.meaning: The traditional count of the parts of the human body; here it means studying with the whole body, aloud.

eruvin-54a-21-24.note: Rav Yosef held a grievance against Rava. On the eve of Yom Kippur Rava decided to go and make peace with him. He found Rav Yosef's attendant mixing him a cup of wine, took the cup and mixed it himself. Rav Yosef, who was blind, tasted it and said it was like Rava's mixing; Rava said: it is I. Rav Yosef told him not to sit down until he explained the verses about the journey from the wilderness to Mattanah, Nahaliel, Bamoth and the valley. Rava explained: a person who makes himself humble like the wilderness receives the Torah as a gift and rises to greatness; if he grows proud, God brings him low, and if he repents, God raises him again.
eruvin-54a-21-24.why: Rav Mattana has just read the same verse, 'from the wilderness to Mattanah', as teaching that Torah lasts only for the humble. The story carries that teaching further, in a scene that is itself about Rava humbling himself.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Son of Rav Yosef bar Hama; went to make peace with Rav Yosef on the eve of Yom Kippur.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A blind Sage who had a grievance against Rava.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement; on its eve people seek forgiveness from anyone they have wronged.
Wine was then strong and was mixed with water before drinking; each person's mixing could be recognized by taste.
Places on the Israelites' route in the Book of Numbers; their names sound like the Hebrew for gift, God's inheritance, and heights.

eruvin-54b-3-3.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was so absorbed in Torah study that he would sit learning in the lower market of Tzippori while his cloak lay in the upper market. Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elazar reported that once a man came to take the cloak and found a serpent on it.
eruvin-54b-3-3.why: The Gemara is reading the verse 'be you ravished always with her love' as praise for love of Torah that makes a person forget the world, and Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat is given as the example.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat
people.about: A Sage so lost in study that he left his cloak in another part of the market.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elazar
people.about: Sage who reports what happened when a man tried to take the cloak.

terms.meaning: A town in the Galilee with an upper and a lower marketplace.

eruvin-54b-19-21.note: Rabbi Perida had a student who needed every lesson taught four hundred times before he learned it. One day Rabbi Perida was called to a mitzva after the lesson, and this time four hundred repetitions were not enough. The student explained that once he heard his teacher was needed elsewhere, he kept thinking, now the master will get up and go. Rabbi Perida told him to pay attention and taught him another four hundred times. A Divine Voice then asked Rabbi Perida whether he would rather have four hundred years added to his life, or that he and his generation merit the World-to-Come. He chose the World-to-Come, and God said: give him both.
eruvin-54b-19-21.why: The discussion has turned to how Torah is learned and reviewed, with Moses teaching the Torah to everyone directly; Rabbi Perida's patience is the Gemara's example of repetition taken to the extreme.

people.name: Rabbi Perida
people.about: A Sage who taught a slow student each lesson four hundred times.

people.name: the student
people.about: Rabbi Perida's student, who needed four hundred repetitions to learn.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who grants Rabbi Perida both rewards.

terms.meaning: A religious duty, such as a communal obligation, for which Rabbi Perida's presence was requested.
A voice from heaven, the Gemara's way of describing a message from God.
The reward of the righteous after this life.

eruvin-60a-6-6.note: Residents of the town of Kakunya asked Rav Yosef to send someone to set up an eiruv for their town. He sent Abaye, warning him to make sure there would be no outcry against it in the study hall. Abaye saw some houses that opened onto the river rather than the town and decided they could be the part left outside the eiruv. Then he changed his mind again and again: such houses do not qualify, so he would cut windows to link them; windows are unnecessary, as Rabba bar Avuh's eiruv in Meḥoza shows; that case is different, so windows are needed; and finally, windows are not needed, since a straw storehouse in Pumbedita once served as the part left out.
eruvin-60a-6-6.why: The mishna says a public city that became private may not have one eiruv for all of it unless a section is left out. Abaye's reversals show how hard that rule is to apply, and afterward he grasps Rav Yosef's warning.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sends Abaye to make the eiruv and warns him to avoid criticism

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sent to make the eiruv; keeps reversing his ruling

people.name: Rabba bar Avuh
people.about: Made an eiruv for Meḥoza neighborhood by neighborhood

people.name: Mar bar Pofidata
people.about: Owned the straw storehouse left outside Pumbedita's eiruv

terms.meaning: A legal arrangement that joins many homes into one shared domain, so that carrying is permitted there on Shabbat.
A part of the town deliberately left out of the eiruv, as the mishna requires for a town that was once public.
The early code of Jewish law on which the Talmud's discussion is built.

eruvin-61a-12-12.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had allowed the people of Geder, a town at the top of a slope, to go down to Hamtan on Shabbat, but did not let the people of Hamtan go up to Geder. When Rav Dimi came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia, he explained the real reason: the people of Geder used to assault the people of Hamtan. So the rule was not a ruling about Shabbat limits at all but an ordinance Rabbi made to keep the peace.
eruvin-61a-12-12.why: Rav Yosef had cited the Geder and Hamtan rule as proof that a town on a slope measures its Shabbat limit from a barrier it builds. Rav Dimi's report takes that proof away, and the Gemara goes on to ask why such an ordinance would apply only on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and reported the true reason behind Rabbi's rule.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he permitted the people of Geder to go down to Hamtan but not the reverse.

terms.meaning: On Shabbat a person may walk only a set distance, two thousand cubits, beyond the place where he is staying. The discussion is about where that distance is measured from.
A rule the Sages made for the public good, as opposed to a ruling that follows from the law itself.

eruvin-63a-7-8.note: Rabbi Elazar from Hagronya and Rav Abba bar Tahalifa visited Rav Aha son of Rav Ika, in the town where Rav Aha bar Ya'akov was the authority. Their host wanted to slaughter a choice third-born calf for them and showed them the knife. Rav Aha bar Tahalifa asked whether they should not show it to the Elder of the town out of respect. Rabbi Elazar answered that Rava had said a Torah scholar may examine a knife for himself, and he examined it. He was later punished by Heaven.
eruvin-63a-7-8.why: The Gemara has just cited Rava's ruling that a Torah scholar may check a slaughtering knife himself. This story shows its limit: once the local Elder's honor had been raised, ignoring him was punished, as the Gemara goes on to explain.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar from Hagronya
people.about: A visiting Sage who checked the knife himself, relying on Rava's ruling, and was punished for it.

people.name: Rav Abba bar Tahalifa
people.about: His travelling companion, who asked whether they should show the knife to the town's Elder. The English also calls him Rav Aha bar Tahalifa.

people.name: Rav Aha son of Rav Ika
people.about: Their host, who wanted to slaughter a calf for them.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov
people.about: The Elder, the senior authority of the town where this happened.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage whose ruling Rabbi Elazar cited: a Torah scholar may examine a knife for himself.

terms.meaning: A calf considered a delicacy; the translation explains its meat was prized.
A knife for ritual slaughter must be perfectly smooth, so it was customary to show it to the local Sage for inspection before use.

eruvin-63a-11-12.note: Ravina was sitting before his teacher Rav Ashi when he saw a man tying his donkey to a palm tree on Shabbat. He shouted at him, but the man paid no attention, and Ravina declared the man excommunicated. Afterward Ravina asked Rav Ashi whether acting like that in his presence looked disrespectful. Rav Ashi quoted the verse "There is no wisdom or understanding or counsel against the Lord": where God's name is being desecrated, no respect is paid even to a teacher.
eruvin-63a-11-12.why: Rava teaches that a student may not rule on law in his teacher's presence, except to stop someone doing something forbidden. Ravina's case illustrates that exception, and the discussion then turns to the punishment for a student who rules before his teacher.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A student who rebuked and excommunicated a Shabbat violator while sitting before his teacher.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Ravina's teacher, who approved of what he did.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who rules that a student may rule in his teacher's presence to stop a transgression.

terms.meaning: A ban placed on a person by a Sage, cutting him off from normal dealings with the community until he mends his ways.
The Sages forbade making use of a growing tree on Shabbat, such as tying an animal to it.
Conduct that brings disrespect on God or His law in public view.

eruvin-63a-15-15.note: One of Rabbi Eliezer's students issued a legal ruling in his teacher's presence. Rabbi Eliezer said to his wife, Imma Shalom, that he would be surprised if this student lived out the year. And the student did not complete his year.
eruvin-63a-15-15.why: The Gemara has just cited Rabbi Eliezer's teaching that Aaron's sons died for ruling before Moses. This case backs the teaching that ruling in a teacher's presence carries a death penalty, and the Gemara then argues over how far away the student actually was.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage whose student ruled on law in front of him; he predicted the student would not survive the year.

people.name: Imma Shalom
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's wife, to whom he made the prediction.

terms.term: issuing a ruling in one's teacher's presence
terms.meaning: Deciding a point of law in front of one's own teacher, which the Sages treated as a grave disrespect.
Lives until the end of the year.

eruvin-63b-10-13.note: A gentile named Lahman bar Ristak lived in an alleyway with Jewish neighbors. They asked him to rent them his rights in the alleyway so they could carry there on Shabbat, but he refused. They went to Abaye, who told them all to give up their rights in favor of one of them, so that a single Jew would be living with a gentile, a case where the gentile does not forbid carrying. They objected that this rule exists only because such living arrangements are rare, and here many people live there. Abaye answered that many people renouncing in favor of one is itself rare, and the Sages made no decree for rare cases.
eruvin-63b-10-13.why: The Gemara returns here to renting a gentile's rights for an eiruv. Abaye's advice is a way around a gentile who will not rent, and when it is reported to Rava he objects that it would make the eiruv look unnecessary.

people.name: Lahman bar Ristak
people.about: A gentile living in the alleyway who would not rent his rights to his Jewish neighbors.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage the neighbors consulted, who suggested they all renounce their rights in favor of one person.

terms.meaning: An arrangement set up before Shabbat that joins neighbors' homes into one shared area, so they may carry objects in a common courtyard or alleyway.
A gentile neighbor cannot join an eiruv, so Jews rent his rights in the shared space from him to let them carry there.
Giving up one's rights in a shared courtyard or alleyway to another resident, leaving fewer people who need to be joined.

eruvin-64a-0-2.note: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua went and told Rava of Abaye's ruling that Jews sharing an alleyway with a gentile could all give up their rights to one of them, who could then carry there. Rava objected that this would abolish the eiruv in that alleyway. Rav Huna answered that they could still make an eiruv as a reminder; Rava said people would then think an eiruv works even where a gentile lives. Rav Huna said they would make an announcement; Rava retorted: will you make an announcement for the children?
eruvin-64a-0-2.why: Abaye has just told the Jewish neighbors of a gentile to give up their rights in the alleyway to one person; this exchange rejects that solution, and Rava then offers his own: borrowing a place from the gentile.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Reports Abaye's ruling to Rava and defends it

people.name: Rava
people.about: Raises objection after objection to the ruling

terms.meaning: A legal arrangement that joins homes into one shared domain so that carrying is permitted on Shabbat; a gentile resident who has not rented out his share blocks it.
Renouncing one's share in a shared space for Shabbat, so that others may carry there.

eruvin-64b-4-9.note: Rabban Gamliel was riding a donkey from Akko to Keziv, with his student Rabbi Elai walking behind. He found loaves of bread on the road and told Elai to pick them up, then met a gentile and said: Mavgai, take these loaves from Elai. Elai asked the man his name and whether Rabban Gamliel had ever met him. It was Mavgai, and they had never met, so they learned Rabban Gamliel had spoken by divine inspiration. At Keziv a man came to have a vow released. Rabban Gamliel confirmed with Elai that they had drunk a quarter-log of Italian wine and told the man to follow them until the wine wore off. After three mil, at the Ladder of Tyre, he got down, wrapped himself in his shawl, sat, and released the vow.
eruvin-64b-4-9.why: Rami bar Abba has just said that walking a mil dispels the effect of wine. This story seems to show it takes three mil, and the Gemara answers that Italian wine is stronger.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Sage riding to Keziv, who knew a stranger's name and later released a man's vow.

people.name: Rabbi Elai
people.about: Rabban Gamliel's student, walking behind him.

people.name: Mavgai
people.about: A gentile from the nearby towns of guardsmen, who was given the loaves.

terms.meaning: A Sage may dissolve a person's vow after hearing him out; the story shows he did it only sober and seated.
A small measure of liquid, roughly a large cupful.
A measure of distance, about two thousand cubits, a little under a kilometer.
A gift of insight from God; here, knowing a stranger's name without being told.

eruvin-65b-14-17.note: Reish Lakish and the students of Rabbi Hanina came to an inn on Shabbat. A gentile tenant there was away, but the gentile landlord was present. They wondered whether they could rent the tenant's rights from the landlord, who had the power to remove him but had not done so. Reish Lakish said: let us rent now, and ask our Sages in the South when we get there. Later they asked Rabbi Afes, who told them they had acted well.
eruvin-65b-14-17.why: The discussion is about when a gentile's presence forbids carrying and who can rent out his rights for an eiruv. This case asks whether a landlord can rent out a tenant's room, and the Gemara follows it with a second inn story about renting on Shabbat itself.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage travelling with the students of Rabbi Hanina, who decided they should rent and ask later.

people.name: Rabbi Afes
people.about: One of the Sages in the South, who approved what they did.

terms.meaning: An arrangement set up before Shabbat that joins neighbors' homes into one shared area, so they may carry objects in a common courtyard.
A gentile cannot join an eiruv, so Jews living with him rent his rights in the shared space to be allowed to carry.

eruvin-65b-18-20.note: Rabbi Hanina bar Yosef, Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Asi came to an inn, and the gentile innkeeper arrived on Shabbat. They asked whether they could rent his rights then. Rabbi Hanina bar Yosef said to rent; Rabbi Asi said not to; Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba said they should rely on the Elder, Rabbi Hanina bar Yosef, and rent. Later they asked Rabbi Yohanan, who said they had acted well. The Sages of Neharde'a wondered whether Rabbi Yohanan had really said this, since he had also said that renting is like making an eiruv.
eruvin-65b-18-20.why: It follows a similar inn case about renting from a landlord. The Gemara then reconciles Rabbi Yohanan's two statements: renting is like an eiruv only in its leniencies, such as a tiny payment or renting from a gentile's hired worker.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina bar Yosef
people.about: The Elder of the group, who said they should rent.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: He said to follow the Elder and rent.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: He said they should not rent.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage they asked afterward, who said they had acted well.

people.name: Sages of Neharde'a
people.about: Scholars who questioned whether Rabbi Yohanan had really said this.

terms.meaning: An arrangement that joins neighbors' homes into one shared area for carrying on Shabbat; it must be set up before Shabbat begins.
Giving up one's rights in a shared courtyard to the other residents, which may be done even on Shabbat.

eruvin-68a-12-12.note: On Shabbat the warm water prepared for a baby's circumcision spilled. Rava had water in his courtyard, but had not joined his courtyard with the baby's by an eiruv. He told those who asked him to move his belongings from the men's room, which opened onto his courtyard, into the inner women's room. He would sit there and renounce his rights in his courtyard in favor of the baby's household, so the water could be carried across. The text does not say what happened next.
eruvin-68a-12-12.why: The Gemara is telling a run of cases about the baby whose water spilled. Ravina then asks how Rava could do this when Shmuel said rights cannot be renounced from one courtyard to another, and Rava says he follows Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who offered to give up his rights in his courtyard so the water could reach the baby.

terms.meaning: An arrangement set up before Shabbat that joins neighbors' homes or courtyards into one area, so objects may be carried between them.
Giving up one's share in a courtyard to others, so that they count as its only residents and may carry there.
A baby's circumcision is done on the eighth day even when that falls on Shabbat; warm water was used to wash the baby.

eruvin-68b-0-3.note: A baby's warm water for his Shabbat circumcision had spilled, and Rava offered to give up his rights to his own courtyard so water could be carried over from it. Ravina challenged him: didn't Shmuel say rights cannot be given up from one courtyard to another? Rava said he followed Rabbi Yoḥanan on that. Ravina asked why, then, Rava did not stay where he was, give up his rights, and have the others give theirs back to him afterward, as Rav allows. Rava said that on this he followed Shmuel, who forbids it. Ravina pressed that both rulings rest on one reason; Rava answered that Shmuel's reason here is different: so that the Sages' rules do not become a joke.
eruvin-68b-0-3.why: The Gemara has been telling of spilled circumcision water on Shabbat; Rava's plan leads into the question whether rights can be given up and given back, which the Gemara then takes up as a dispute between Rav and Shmuel.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Challenges Rava's plan with Shmuel's rulings

people.name: Rava
people.about: Plans to give up his rights to his courtyard so the baby's water can be carried

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage whose rulings on giving up rights are quoted

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Sage who allows giving up rights from one courtyard to another

terms.term: giving up rights to a courtyard
terms.meaning: On Shabbat, a resident who did not join the eiruv can renounce his share in a shared courtyard so that others may carry there.
A legal arrangement that joins homes and courtyards into one shared domain so that carrying is permitted on Shabbat.

eruvin-68b-13-16.note: Rabban Gamliel recalled a Sadducee who lived in the same alleyway in Jerusalem as his family and had given up his rights in it before Shabbat. His father told them to hurry and take their utensils out into the alleyway before the Sadducee took his out and forbade it to them. In a version taught by Rabbi Meir, Rabban Gamliel told his sons to hurry and carry what they needed before that loathsome man took out his things. Rabbi Yehuda reports his words differently: hurry and do what you need in the alleyway before night falls.
eruvin-68b-13-16.why: The mishna asks whether a Sadducee, who rejects the Sages' traditions, counts as a gentile for an eiruv. The Gemara says Rabban Gamliel told this incident to show he does not, and then works through Rabbi Meir's and Rabbi Yehuda's versions.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: He tells of a Sadducee who shared his family's alleyway; in one version he urges his sons to hurry.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage whose version of Rabban Gamliel's words is quoted first.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: He gives a different version of what Rabban Gamliel said.

terms.meaning: A member of a Jewish group that rejected the Sages' oral traditions.
A member of a group close to the Sadducees, likewise rejecting the Sages' traditions.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
Gave up his share in the shared alleyway so the others could carry there on Shabbat.

eruvin-69a-8-8.note: A man went out into the public street on Shabbat wearing a coral ring, which is forbidden. When he saw Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, he covered it. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia said that someone like this may renounce his rights in a courtyard, according to Rabbi Yehuda.
eruvin-69a-8-8.why: The Gemara has just said, following Rabbi Yehuda, that only a Jew who breaks Shabbat brazenly in public is barred from renouncing his rights. A man who hides his transgression shows who falls on the other side of that line.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: The Sage the man saw; he judged that the man may still renounce his rights.

terms.meaning: Give up his share in a shared courtyard so his neighbors may carry there on Shabbat. A Jew who openly breaks Shabbat is treated like a gentile and cannot do this.
Wearing such an ornament into the public domain on Shabbat counts as carrying it, which is forbidden.

eruvin-74a-7-7.note: Ivut bar Ihi lived in an alleyway that had only one house and one courtyard. He put up a side post for it, and Shmuel permitted him to carry there. Later Rav Anan came and threw the side post down. Ivut bar Ihi said with resentment: shall Rav Anan bar Rav come and throw it down from the alleyway where I have been living and walking by Master Shmuel's ruling?
eruvin-74a-7-7.why: When Rabbi Elazar challenged Shmuel's ruling that such an alleyway can be permitted with a side post, Shmuel fell silent. The Gemara uses this story to argue he never retracted, then rejects the proof: a synagogue attendant slept there, so the alley had two residences.

people.name: Ivut bar Ihi
people.about: A man who lived in the alleyway and put up a side post on Shmuel's ruling.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who permitted Ivut to carry in his alleyway.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: Also called Rav Anan bar Rav; he came and threw the side post down.

terms.meaning: A post set up at the open end of an alleyway that marks it off so residents may carry within it on Shabbat. Normally it works only for an alleyway with at least two courtyards.

eruvin-80a-6-12.note: Rabbi Oshaya's daughter-in-law went to a bathhouse beyond the Shabbat limit before Shabbat, and it grew dark before she could return. Her mother-in-law set up an eiruv for her so she could come home. The case came before Rabbi Hiyya, who forbade it. Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei said to him: Babylonian, are you so strict about eiruv? My father said, wherever you can be lenient with eiruv, be lenient. The Sages later asked why it had been invalid. Rabbi Ya'akov, sent by Rabbi Zeira to ask Rav Ya'akov bar Idi, was told it was the mother-in-law's food and she had not given her daughter-in-law ownership of it.
eruvin-80a-6-12.why: Rav holds that food for a Shabbat-limit eiruv must be formally given to the people it serves. The Gemara says this is an old dispute and cites Rabbi Hiyya's ruling in this case as Rav's source.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: His daughter-in-law was caught outside the Shabbat limit.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The Sage who ruled the mother-in-law's eiruv invalid.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: He rebuked Rabbi Hiyya for being too strict, quoting his father.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov
people.about: Also called son of the daughter of Ya'akov; he reported Rabbi Yohanan's explanation and was sent to ask Rav Ya'akov bar Idi.

people.name: Rav Ya'akov bar Idi
people.about: The Sage at the Ladder of Tyre who explained why the eiruv had failed.

terms.meaning: On Shabbat a person may walk only two thousand cubits beyond the place where he is staying.
A kind of eiruv: food placed before Shabbat at a spot that then counts as one's home base, letting one walk further from there.
Formally giving the eiruv food to the people it is meant for, usually through someone who receives it on their behalf.

eruvin-85b-18-18.note: The son of Bonyas, a very rich man, came before Rabbi, who told his attendants: make way for one worth a hundred maneh. Another man came, and Rabbi said: make way for one worth two hundred maneh. Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei said: Rabbi, this one's father has a thousand ships at sea and a thousand towns on land. Rabbi answered: when you reach his father, tell him not to send him to me in these clothes. The Gemara comments that Rabbi and Rabbi Akiva both honored the wealthy.
eruvin-85b-18-18.why: The mishna's "right of usage" was just explained by the courtyard of Bonyas, a rich man who kept his goods in his tenants' rooms. The Gemara adds this second Bonyas story before going back to the law.

people.name: son of Bonyas
people.about: Son of an extremely wealthy man; he came before Rabbi in clothes that did not show his wealth.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who seated his visitors by their apparent wealth.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: He told Rabbi how rich the young man's father was.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Mentioned by the Gemara as another Sage who honored the wealthy.

terms.meaning: A large sum of money, one hundred zuz; a hundred maneh means great wealth.

eruvin-86b-9-11.note: Rav Dimi reported an incident in Tzippori. The people forgot to bring a Torah scroll to the synagogue before Shabbat. The next day they spread a sheet over the pillars between the house where the scroll was kept and the synagogue, brought the scroll through, and read from it. The Gemara at once questions this telling: may one spread a sheet on Shabbat, when everyone agrees a temporary tent may not be put up then?
eruvin-86b-9-11.why: The Gemara is asking whether Rabbi Yosei relied on hanging partitions for carrying on Shabbat. It says the Tzippori incident followed his son, Rabbi Yishmael, not him, and then rereads it as sheets that were already spread.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and reported the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage on whose authority the Gemara says the Tzippori incident was done.

terms.meaning: A wall that hangs down without reaching the ground, such as a sheet; the question is whether it counts as a real wall for carrying on Shabbat.
Putting up any covering on Shabbat, even a temporary one, counts as building and is forbidden.

eruvin-91a-1-3.note: Rabbi recalled that when he and others studied Torah with Rabbi Shimon in Tekoa, they would carry oil and a towel from roof to roof, roof to courtyard, courtyard to courtyard and through enclosures until they reached the spring where they bathed. Rabbi Yehuda told of a time of danger when they carried a Torah scroll from courtyard to roof, roof to courtyard and courtyard to enclosure, in order to read from it.
eruvin-91a-1-3.why: Rav Yehuda has just set out the views of Rabbi Meir, the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon on carrying between roofs, courtyards and enclosures. These memories support his reading of Rabbi Shimon; the Sages answer that a time of danger proves nothing.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, recalling what he and his fellow students did while studying with Rabbi Shimon.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The teacher in Tekoa with whom they studied.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who told of carrying a Torah scroll in a time of danger.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Named in the teaching on roofs, which sets out his view.

terms.meaning: A fenced area such as a yard or storage lot that is not lived in; it has its own rules for carrying on Shabbat.
A period, the translation explains, when decrees banned religious practice.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

eruvin-94a-1-2.note: Rav and Shmuel were sitting in a courtyard on Shabbat when the wall between it and the next courtyard fell. Shmuel told the people to take a cloak and hang it on what was left of the wall. Rav turned his face away. Shmuel said to them, joking: if Abba is particular, take his belt and tie it on.
eruvin-94a-1-2.why: The Gemara says Rav's view, that carrying is limited to four cubits once such a wall falls, was never stated outright but inferred from his turning away here. It then asks why Shmuel needed the cloak and why Rav stayed silent.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Also called Abba; he turned his face away when Shmuel told people to hang the cloak.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: His colleague, who told the people to hang a cloak where the wall had fallen; it was his town.

terms.meaning: Where carrying is not permitted, a person may still move an object within four cubits, about two meters.

eruvin-101b-0-0.note: Rabbi Meir said one may not open a door from one kind of area into another unless one has built a partition ten handbreadths high. The Rabbis answered with an incident from the poultry dealers' market in Jerusalem. The dealers would lock their shops and leave the key in a window above the door. Rabbi Yosei says it was the wool dealers' market.
eruvin-101b-0-0.why: The Gemara asks how the Rabbis could answer Rabbi Meir, who spoke of the public domain, with a Jerusalem market, since Jerusalem had only lesser status. Rava reads this part of the mishna as being about the gates of a garden.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage who required a partition before one could open such a door.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: He says the market in question was that of the wool dealers.

terms.meaning: A measure of about 8 to 10 centimeters; ten handbreadths high is the height that makes a separate area in Shabbat law.
An in-between area, neither fully private nor fully public, where the Sages forbade carrying.

eruvin-102a-14-15.note: Rav Huna kept rams that needed shade during the day and fresh air at night, so their pen had to be covered by day and open by night, Shabbat included. He came to Rav for advice. Rav told him to roll up the mats that shaded the pen but leave one handbreadth still spread; the next day he could unroll the whole mat, since that only adds to a temporary tent that already exists, which is permitted.
eruvin-102a-14-15.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rav Asi: over boat arches a handbreadth wide, a mat may be spread on Shabbat because it only adds to a temporary tent. Rav's advice applies the same principle to an animal pen.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Owner of the rams, who asks Rav how to shade them by day and air them by night.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage Rav Huna consults; he tells him to leave a handbreadth of the mat spread.

terms.meaning: A roof put up for a short time. Building a new one on Shabbat is forbidden, but adding to one that already stands is allowed, which is why leaving a handbreadth in place before Shabbat matters.
A unit of measure, roughly the width of a palm (about 8 to 10 cm). A covering of at least this width counts as a roof in Jewish law.

eruvin-102b-11-12.note: Mar bar Rav Ashi recalls standing before his father, Rav Ashi, when his father's bandage fell onto a pillow and he put it back on. The son asked whether he did not hold by Rav Hisda's teaching that the dispute concerns only a bandage that fell onto a utensil, together with Shmuel's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. His father answered, "I did not hear this," which the Gemara explains as meaning "I do not agree."
eruvin-102b-11-12.why: A baraita disputes whether a bandage that came off may be replaced on Shabbat; Rav Hisda limited the dispute to one that fell onto a utensil, and Shmuel ruled with Rabbi Yehuda. Rav Ashi's conduct shows he rejected Rav Hisda's limit and allowed putting the bandage back.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Son of Rav Ashi, who tells the story and questions his father.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The father, called simply Father here, who replaces his fallen bandage on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Sage whose teaching limits the dispute to a bandage that fell onto a utensil.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage who ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Sage of the earlier baraita whose opinion Shmuel says is the law.

terms.meaning: The binding Jewish law on a question, as opposed to an opinion that was argued but not adopted.

eruvin-104a-13-13.note: Ulla was staying at the house of Rav Menashe on Shabbat when a man came and knocked on the door. Ulla said: Who is that? May his body be desecrated, since he desecrates Shabbat. Rabba told him the Sages forbade only musical sounds on Shabbat, not knocking. Abaye raised an objection to Rabba from a teaching that allows drawing wine with a siphon and dripping water for a sick person on Shabbat; the answer does not come within the story.
eruvin-104a-13-13.why: After the mishna's ruling on drawing water from the Cistern of the Exiles on Shabbat, the Gemara turns to whether making a sound on Shabbat is forbidden; Ulla's curse and Rabba's reply open that debate.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: Visiting Sage who curses the man knocking on Shabbat

people.name: Rav Menashe
people.about: The host at whose house Ulla was staying

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Says only musical sounds are forbidden on Shabbat

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Raises an objection to Rabba's view

terms.meaning: A cistern named in the mishna, from which the mishna allows water to be drawn on Shabbat.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

eruvin-104a-24-25.note: Ameimar allowed the people of Mehoza to draw water on Shabbat with a wheel. He reasoned that the Sages forbade it only in case someone drew water for his garden or his ruin, and Mehoza had neither gardens nor ruins. But once he saw that they were soaking flax in the water, he forbade them to use the wheel.
eruvin-104a-24-25.why: The Gemara has just explained that the mishna limits wheel-drawing to the Temple because of a decree: a person might go on to water his garden. Ameimar's ruling tests that reason in a town where it seemed not to apply.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage who first permits and then forbids drawing water by wheel in Mehoza.

terms.meaning: A rule the Sages added to protect people from breaking a Torah law by accident. Here the worry is that someone using the wheel would also water his garden, which is forbidden work on Shabbat.
Steeping flax plants in water to loosen the fibers for linen. Doing it on Shabbat is forbidden work, so drawing water for it was a real risk.
